content.text:
Judge rows 75-101.

Row 75 (n=180): "I want Oak room renamed to Oak hall" — like n=108. L8.

Row 76 (n=182): "facilities renamed all the rooms after rivers, so the Board room is now Danube"
sop: c1 renamed subject facilities complement n2(all the rooms); r1 marker=after from c1 to n3(rivers); r2 marker=so from c1 to c2; n4 the Board room; c2 declarative verb=is modifier=now subject=n4 complement=n5(Danube). Good. L8.

Row 77 (n=185): "hmm, Focus pod sounds odd to clients - let's go with Think tank instead"
sop: c1 imperative discourse=hmm verb=let complement=n3("'s"); n1 Focus pod; c2 declarative sounds modifier=odd subject=n1; r1 marker=to from c2 to n2(clients); c3 nonfinite verb=go modifier=instead; r2 marker=with from c3 to n4(Think tank); r3 c1→c2; r4 c1→c3. Good — "'s" as complement of let per settled case. L8.

Row 78 (n=186): "ok so the sign outside now says Cedar 2, please update the cedar room to match"
sop: c1 declarative discourse=ok modifier=so modifier=outside modifier=now verb=says subject=n1(sign); n2 Cedar; n3 2; c2 imperative please update complement n4(the cedar room); r1 marker=to from c2 to c3(match nonfinite); k1 coordination conjunct=c1, c4, c2; c4 fragment complement=n2 (Cedar); r2 from n2 to n3.

Hmm, k1 joins three conjuncts: c1 (the sign says...), c4 (fragment "Cedar 2"!), c2 (please update...). c4 is the fragment holding "Cedar"+"2" — which is what the sign says, i.e., the content of "says". Making it a conjunct of the coordination is odd: it states "Cedar 2" is a separate thing put side by side. Also "Cedar 2" as the object of "says" is lost: c1 "says" has no complement; n2 is in c4 fragment. Hmm.

The "so" as modifier of c1: at start, acceptable-ish (discourse preferred but modifier allowed analog for "now"? rule mentions "Now" at start).

Is this L3? The coordination with a fragment conjunct: "the sign outside now says Cedar 2, please update the cedar room to match". The words "Cedar 2" are the content of "says". Writing them as a fragment joined in coordination with the clause of "says" — that's a wrong tie? It states Cedar 2 is coordinated with the clauses instead of being the complement of "says". Hmm, but the coordination c1+c4 at least ties them together; a next layer reading "sign says" then "Cedar 2" as conjunct... it can figure out. Hmm.

But grade-wise: "A coordination has a wrong conjunct" (L3). Is c4 a wrong conjunct? "Cedar 2" cannot be a conjunct of a coordination with clauses — the words don't give a coordination of that fragment. That's stating a tie the message doesn't have (L4 "a coordination between wires that the message does not relate") or L3 wrong conjunct.

Hmm. Careful: "the sign outside now says Cedar 2" — three-way coordination: c1, c4, c2. The message: two sentences joined by comma: "the sign ... says Cedar 2" and "please update ... to match". A coordination of c1 and c2 is fine (rules allow a coordination of the clauses of two sentences). But inserting c4 (a fragment) as a third conjunct between them is a statement the message does not make — the fragment isn't a coordinated unit.

Also is "Cedar 2" properly placed as the thing said? It's tied to nothing except via k1. Effectively c4 is a conjunct, so not "tied to nothing"... 

I think this is a genuine fault: L3 (wrong conjunct). Alternative: L6 (Cedar 2 tied to nothing inside its sentence - it's not "tied to nothing" though: k1 holds it).

Hmm. Which grade? The wrong conjunct is the clearer statement: the coordination holds a fragment that the message does not coordinate. I'll grade L3.

Hmm, but wait: maybe a fairer read: the coordination joins c1 and c2 (two sentences) and c4 joins them too — the fragment being the content of "says" is a plausible-position reading? No, the content should be a complement of the "says" clause.

Also "outside" as modifier of c1 — fine.

Correction:
@c1 syntax.clause form=declarative discourse="ok" modifier="so" modifier="outside" modifier="now" verb="says" subject=$n1 complement=$n2
@n1 syntax.nominal dependent="the" head="sign"
@n2 syntax.nominal dependent="Cedar" head="2"
@c2 syntax.clause form=imperative discourse="please" verb="update" complement=$n4
@n4 syntax.nominal dependent="the" dependent="cedar" head="room"
@r1 syntax.relation marker="to" from=$c2 to=$c3
@c3 syntax.clause form=nonfinite verb="match"
@k1 syntax.coordination conjunct=$c1 conjunct=$c2

Wait "Cedar 2" — hmm, is "2" head with "Cedar" dependent? "Cedar 2" is a name-ish. Allowed ("A name of several words may stand whole in head"). Fine.

Row 79 (n=187): "Board room -> Main room" — fragment n1; c1 fragment modifier=">" complement n1; n2; r1 n1→n2. Fine. L8.

Row 80 (n=193): "Cedar room, rename to Willow" — c1 imperative rename (no complement), r1 to from c1 to n2(Willow), c2 fragment complement n1(Cedar room), k1 c2 c1. Good. L8.

Row 81 (n=197): "can you update the board room so it seats 16?" — question with "so" clause → c2 declarative, tied by r1 marker so from c1 to c2. Good. L8.

Row 82 (n=199): "Focus pod capacity should be 3 people" — c1 aux should verb be subject n1(Focus pod capacity) complement n2(3 people). Good. L8.

Row 83 (n=201): "we moved two extra chairs into the Focus pod, so it holds 4 people now" — good. L8.

Row 84 (n=202): "because of the new distancing rules, the Board room can only take 9 people - please update it"
sop: r1 marker=because from c1 to n1; n1 nominal head="of"; n2 = "the new distancing rules"; n3 = the Board room; c1 declarative aux=can modifier=only verb=take subject=n3 complement=n2 complement=n4;

Hmm: n1 with head "of" — "of" is written as a nominal's head. That's wrong: "of" is a linking word, not a noun. And "the new distancing rules" is a complement of c1 (take), which is wrong — "take 9 people" — the object is 9 people; "the rules" belongs to the "because of" phrase.

Faults: "of" as a head of a nominal (n1) — the words "because of the new distancing rules" form one phrase: "because" marker, "of" ... hmm. Actually "because of" is a two-word preposition. Then "the new distancing rules" is its object. r1 marker=because from c1 to n1(head "of")? That's broken: "of" held as a nominal head. This is L3 ("A linking word is held as a modifier or a dependent" — here held as a head; arguably same spirit. Also "words of one nominal are split between wires, or two nominals are merged", "The head is wrong").

Also n2 (the new distancing rules) is made a complement of "take" — a nominal that is the complement of the wrong clause? It's the object of "because of", not of "take" → L3.

So L3 for n=202. Quote: 'because of the new distancing rules'. Correction:
@c1 syntax.clause form=declarative auxiliary="can" modifier="only" verb="take" subject=$n3 complement=$n4
@n1 syntax.nominal dependent="the" dependent="new" dependent="distancing" head="rules"
@r1 syntax.relation marker="because of" from=$c1 to=$n1
@n3 syntax.nominal dependent="the" dependent="Board" head="room"
@n4 syntax.nominal dependent="9" head="people"
@c2 syntax.clause form=imperative discourse="please" verb="update" complement=$n5
@n5 syntax.nominal head="it"
@r2 syntax.relation from=$c2 to=$c1

Hmm, marker "because of" as two words — allowed? "right on" allowed merging. I'd rather do: marker="because" from c1 to n1 where n1 = "of the new distancing rules"? That's what sop did (n1 head "of"). Not good. Better: "because of" as one marker with n1 = "the new distancing rules". I'll use marker="because of".

Row 85 (n=203): "the Cedar room got the big table back. Could you bump it up to 12 seats?" — good. L8.

Row 86 (n=206): "hey, the Oak room was rebuilt - it's got space for 30 people now"
sop: c1 declarative discourse=hey aux='s verb=got modifier=now subject=n2(it) complement=n3(space); r1 marker=for from n3 to n4(30 people); c2 declarative aux=was verb=rebuilt subject=n1(the Oak room); r2 from c1 to c2. Words: hey the Oak room was rebuilt it 's got space for 30 people now. All covered? "the","Oak","room" n1; "was" c2 aux; "rebuilt" c2 verb; "it" n2; "'s" c1 aux; "got" c1 verb; "space" n3; "for" marker; "30","people" n4; "now" c1 modifier. Yes. L8.

Row 87 (n=209): "it seats 5" — L8.

Row 88 (n=210): "focus pod, capacity 2 please" — n1 focus pod, n2 capacity, n3 2; c1 fragment please complement n1; r1 n1→n2; r2 n2→n3. Good. L8.

Row 89 (n=215): "the Board room is now in building C" — fine. L8.

Row 90 (n=218): "please update the cedar room: it's next to the kitchen now"
sop: c1 imperative please update complement n1; c2 declarative verb='s modifier=now subject=it; r1 marker="next to" from c2 to n3(the kitchen); k1 coordination c1 c2. Good ("next to" as one marker is fine). L8.

Row 91 (n=221): "we swapped floors with marketing, so the Focus pod is up on the 6th floor now" — L8.

Row 92 (n=223): "move the Cedar room to building A and rename it Cedar A" — L8.

Row 93 (n=224): "guests can't find the focus pod; would you note that it's behind reception, past the coffee machine?"
sop: c1 declarative aux=ca negation=n't verb=find subject=guests complement=n2; c2 interrogative would note subject you; r1 marker=that from c2 to c3; c3 declarative verb='s subject=it; r2 marker=behind from c3 to n5(reception); r3 marker=past from c3 to n6(coffee machine); k1 coordination c1 c2. Good. L8.

Row 94 (n=225): "if the Oak room really is in the basement now, please update where it is"
sop: r1 marker=if from c2 to c1; c1 declarative really is now subject n1; r2 marker=in from c1 to n2(basement); c2 imperative please update (no complement); c3 declarative modifier=where verb=is subject=it; r3 from c2 to c3.
"where it is" — clause opening with a question word inside another clause: per settled case its form is declarative and tied to the clause it belongs to (r3 ✓). "where" held as modifier of c3 — settled case: a question word "stands where grammar puts it: ... a modifier in 'where is it?'". OK. L8.

Row 95 (n=226): "ok so after the office move the Board room is at 40 King Street, 2nd floor - can you fix that?"
sop: c1 declarative discourse=ok modifier=so verb=is subject=n2(the Board room); r1 marker=after from c1 to n1(the office move); r2 marker=at from c1 to n3(40 King Street); n4(2nd floor); c2 interrogative can fix subject you complement that; k1 coordination c1 c2; r3 from n3 to n4. Good. L8.

Row 96 (n=227): "this room moved upstairs"
sop: c1 form=nonfinite verb=moved modifier=upstairs subject=n1(this room).
Fault: "this room moved upstairs" is a declarative sentence with a subject and a finite verb "moved" (past tense). Written as nonfinite → form wrong. Is nonfinite→declarative in L1's list? L1 lists "a clear question written as imperative or declarative, or the reverse; a clause with a verb written as fragment". Nonfinite is a third category. Hmm. "this room moved upstairs" — a full statement; writing it nonfinite says the clause cannot make a sentence by itself, which is a wrong statement about the clause's form. I'd call L1: form is wrong for a plain declarative statement.

Hmm, careful about consistency: earlier I accepted declarative for nonfinite subordinate clauses (row 8's "getting mixed up"). Direction matters: writing a full finite statement as nonfinite is a stronger error (it denies the sentencehood of the message's only clause), and it also breaks the "form" of the message's main clause. I'll grade L1 for n=227.

Hmm, but is it? Let me think about the next-layer test. "this room moved upstairs": c1 nonfinite verb=moved, subject=this room. The next layer learns: a thing ("this room") moved upstairs. Is anything lost? Not much semantically. Only the form label. Compare with L1's spirit: the form of a clause must be right. A declarative sentence written nonfinite — the rules' examples of L1 form errors are question↔declarative and verb-bearing clause as fragment. Both of those are cases where the next layer misreads the type of the message. Here the message is a statement; the circuit says "nonfinite" — the next layer knows the verb and subject. Hmm.

I'm torn. Consider consistency: for row 97 (n=233) "Board room moved to floor 9" the sop also writes nonfinite. Same question.

Let me think about which is more likely the rules' intent. The grade table's L1 first item: "A clause that the circuit writes is wrong. Its `form` is wrong: a clear question written as `imperative` or `declarative`, or the reverse; a clause with a verb written as `fragment`." The examples given are the types of form errors they consider. The "or the reverse" of "a clear question written as declarative" is "a declarative written as interrogative" — which I used for n=150 and n=56-like cases. Nonfinite/fragment confusion is separately mentioned (verb as fragment). So nonfinite written as declarative, or declarative written as nonfinite, isn't enumerated... but the general statement is "Its form is wrong".

I think the honest judge position: writing the message's only, finite clause as `nonfinite` is a wrong statement about the clause (it says the words cannot make a sentence, which they do). That's L1. I'll apply it to n=227 and n=233 consistently. But then should I also reject row 8's c2 (declarative for the nonfinite "getting mixed up")? There, a genuinely nonfinite part was labeled declarative — the mirror, and it also is "form wrong". Hmm. If I reject one direction I should reject the other for consistency... but I already wrote n=8 as L8. I could revise n=8 later — but I'd rather not.

Alternative consistent policy: form labels on subordinate/participial clauses are lenient (either passes), EXCEPT where the whole message's main clause form is at stake (question vs statement vs command). Under that policy:
- n=8 c2 declarative (subordinate passive) → OK.
- n=227 "this room moved upstairs" — the message's only clause, a statement, written nonfinite → the main clause's form is wrong. Hmm, but is it "wrong" in a way that misleads? The next layer sees a nonfinite clause with a subject; it wouldn't think it's a question or a command. The distinction that matters for the next layer is question/statement/command, which is preserved ("nonfinite with a subject" is odd but not a false claim about questionhood).

Ugh. Let me look at whether these rows also have another defect. n=227: eventually "this room moved upstairs" — hmm, "upstairs" as modifier of the clause ✓. No other defect.

I think the rules intend form to be one of the things judged, and a nonfinite label on a finite sentence is a real form error. The settled cases show them being picky about form in similar situations ("Written as a command, imperative, passes too" etc.). But they also show leniency for ambiguous cases.

Decision: I'll treat "a clause whose words give a plain finite statement but written `nonfinite`" as L1, and apply it to n=227, n=233 (if similar), and check others. Wait — n=233 "Board room moved to floor 9" same construction. And row 96 also. Both from same formalizer probably in this packet.

Hmm, but hold on: is there an argument that "moved" here could be read as a participle, i.e., the message is a fragment describing a moved state ("this room [moved upstairs]")? "this room moved upstairs" — as English, it is a complete sentence. Could be a note "this room moved upstairs" = statement. So form should be declarative.

Hmm, but see settled case: "A message or a part with no verb ('pie radius smaller', 'legend on the right', 'a fireplace') is a fragment." These have a verb, so declarative.

I'll go L1 for 227 and 233. Actually wait. Let me reconsider the risk balance. The judge instruction says "Judge fairly: a plausible or incomplete reading that the next layer can continue from is acceptable; reject only a wrong statement or lost explicit information." Is "nonfinite" for "this room moved upstairs" a wrong statement? It labels the clause's form wrongly — that IS a wrong statement, and it's exactly what L1 covers ("Its form is wrong"). But is it "a wrong statement the next layer must undo"? The next layer would read: a clause with verb "moved", subject "this room", nonfinite, tied to nothing (no relation holds c1!). Ah — interesting: c1 is a standalone clause with no relation; a nonfinite clause tied to nothing is L6 per settled case! "A participle or a subordinate clause tied to nothing is L6."

So n=227: c1 nonfinite, tied to nothing → L6 (and form L1). Which first? L1 < L6, so L1.

Hmm, that strengthens the rejection: a nonfinite clause tied to nothing is at least L6. So reject.

For n=233: c1 nonfinite "moved", tied by r1 (marker=to) to n2 — so it's tied. So only the form issue remains. Hmm, then if I grade L1 there it's purely on the form. Hmm.

Let me decide: for n=233, "Board room moved to floor 9" written as nonfinite with a subject and a relation — the reading is fine and the clause is tied. Rejecting for form alone feels harsh but the form label is wrong: the message is a statement.

Alternative: treat these as acceptable (L8) since the next layer loses nothing. Hmm.

Let me consider the spirit: L1's purpose is to catch circuits that misstate the sentence's type. A statement labeled nonfinite isn't a question/command confusion; the reader still gets subject+verb+content. I'm now leaning that these two are acceptable (L8), for n=227 too? But n=227's c1 is tied to nothing (a nonfinite clause tied to nothing is L6 per settled case). If instead the clause were declarative (its true form), being a standalone clause tied to nothing is fine (a sentence needs no tie). So the mislabelling creates an L6-ish situation. Hmm — the mislabel alone yields "participle tied to nothing".

I think for n=227, rejecting is justified: the circuit writes the message's whole statement as a nonfinite clause attached to nothing, so it says a fragment floats without a verb-clause of its own. Let me grade L1 with note about form and quote 'this room moved upstairs'. And for n=233 also L1 for consistency (both are "X moved ..." statements written nonfinite). Hmm, but that punishes only-form.

Alternatively grade n=233 as L8 and n=227 as L1 — inconsistent-ish but distinguished by the tie. Hmm, I'd rather be principled: the form of a clause is a judged item (rule 1 in "What must be right"). A finite statement written as nonfinite is a form error. Both get L1. I'll accept the slight risk of harshness; it's a defensible reading of the rules.

Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider once more. There's a risk the intended answer (gold) for such rows is L8, and the note must quote words. My judgment is supposed to be my own fair judgment, not to match a gold. The instructions say reject only a wrong statement or lost information. Writing "nonfinite" where the clause is finite is a wrong statement. OK, L1.

Hmm, but then n=8's c2 (declarative for nonfinite "getting mixed up with work stuff") is also a wrong form statement, and I accepted. Difference: in n=8 the main clause and the sentence type are right; the error is confined to a subordinate verb phrase whose form the labels of that formalizer used loosely. For consistency I could justify: for a subordinate nonfinite part, both labels are tolerated because grammar and the words don't settle it; for the message's own clause with a subject and a finite verb, "nonfinite" contradicts the words.

Hmm, in n=227 c1 has a subject "this room" explicitly. In n=233 too. Supporting the "finite" claim. And in n=8, c2 has no subject → arguably could be read either way. That's a principled distinction: a clause with a subject and a finite verb form cannot be nonfinite. Good, I'll adopt it:

Policy: if a clause carries an explicit `subject` and a finite verb (no "to", not a participle), its form can't be `nonfinite`/`fragment` → form error (L1). If the clause has no subject, nonfinite/declarative labels are lenient.

Wait, but that conflicts with row 22's c2 (n=68) "I want the Gym calendar gone": c2 nonfinite verb=gone subject=n2 — that's a nonfinite clause with a subject (like "Work shown"). Form nonfinite with subject is fine there because "gone" is a participle. Yes fine: participle = nonfinite.

And n=233 "moved": "moved" is past tense finite; could "moved" be a participle? "Board room moved to floor 9" — participle reading would be a fragment "Board room [moved to floor 9]" (like "board room moved"). Ambiguous! Hmm! Actually "board room moved to floor 9" as a note could be a reduced relative/fragment: "board room, moved to floor 9". But there's no comma. In these terse note-style messages, "X moved to Y" is a statement.

Ugh, this is genuinely ambiguous. Given ambiguity (a word that grammar allows as finite or participle), the rules' leniency principle ("plausible or incomplete reading ... is acceptable") applies. Hmm! Then n=227 and n=233: "moved" can be read as participle, with the subject written — hmm, a participle clause with a subject is odd, but the settled case allows "a group called g2", "a bird facing left" (no subject). 

Hmm, this ambiguity pushes toward L8 for n=233 and L6/L1 for n=227? For n=227, if "moved" is a participle, then the whole message is a nonfinite clause tied to nothing = L6 (settled: "A participle or a subordinate clause tied to nothing is L6"). Either way n=227 is rejected: if finite → L1 (form), if participle → L6. Which grade to give? The safer/most defensible: L6? Hmm, but the primary fault if finite is the form.

Let me pick: n=227 → L6 (participle tied to nothing; the sentence "this room moved upstairs" is a statement of its own that needs no tie). Hmm, but if I say "the message is a statement, and the circuit writes it as a nonfinite clause tied to nothing" → that combines both. Which grade is "first that applies"? L1 (form) comes before L6. Hmm.

I'll go with L6 for n=227? No... Let me be decisive: I'll grade n=227 L6 with a note: the message states 'this room moved upstairs' but the circuit writes it as a nonfinite clause ('participle') tied to nothing, so it hangs off no clause. Hmm, but that note really describes L1 form + L6 tie. Since the note must "name the wrong statement or the lost information", and the grade should be the first applicable... 

I'll give L1 for n=227: "moved" is the finite verb of the message's only clause, yet the clause is written `nonfinite`, so the statement is turned into a dangling participle. And n=233 L8? Inconsistent.

OK let me settle this properly with one rule: treat a clause with an explicit subject and a verb that has a finite past/present reading as-is; label `nonfinite` = form error = L1; BUT if the verb form is a participle (ends in -ing/-ed used adjectivally and the message supports a fragment reading), lenient.

"moved" is -ed... both. "this room moved upstairs" - I keep going in circles. 

Decision (final): Accept both as L8? The cost of wrongly rejecting: I'd be unfair to a plausible circuit. The cost of wrongly accepting: a form label wrong. The instruction "Judge fairly: a plausible or incomplete reading that the next layer can continue from is acceptable" tilts toward acceptance. A circuit that reads "this room moved upstairs" as a clause with verb "moved", subject "this room", and label nonfinite — the next layer has the verb and the subject; it can continue fully. Nothing is lost; nothing must be undone except the form label which doesn't mislead about question/command.

Hmm, but n=227's clause tied to nothing: a clause that IS the whole message — "Separate sentences need no tie". Does the L6 rule ("A participle or a subordinate clause tied to nothing is L6") bite? The clause isn't a participle in truth; it's the message's main clause. So no L6.

Final: n=227 L8, n=233 L8. This keeps consistency with n=8 too. Good — simpler policy: form leniency for nonfinite/declarative confusion; strictness only for question/command/statement confusion (imperative/interrogative/declarative) and verb-in-fragment.

Wait, but under that policy, n=150 ("it seats four" interrogative) — that's interrogative vs declarative, which is the explicitly listed error → L1. Good. And n=56/others fine.

So rows 96 (n=227) L8, 97 (n=233) L8.

Row 97 (n=233): also n2 head="floor" with n3 "9" tied by r2 to n2 — "floor 9": fine.

Row 98 (n=236): "please get rid of the board room" — L8.

Row 99 (n=238): "I want the Focus pod removed as a room" — L8.

Row 100 (n=243): "if no one has the Library booked, you can delete that room"
sop: r1 marker=if from c3 to c1; c1 declarative has subject n1(no one); n2 the Library; c2 nonfinite booked subject n2; n3 you; c3 declarative can delete subject you complement n4; r2 c1→c2. Good. L8.

Row 101 (n=244): "the building closed the old Annex for good; would you mind removing it from the rooms?" — c1 closed; r1 marker=for from c1 to n3(good): "for good" as a fixed phrase - a relation marked "for" to "good" — plausible. k1 c1 c2; c2 would mind; c3 nonfinite removing complement it; r2 from c3 to n6; r3 c2→c3. Good. L8.

So this chunk: only n=186 (row 78) and n=202 (row 84) rejected. Let me write part 4.

Wait, double-check row 78 more carefully; also consider whether the "so" as modifier of c1 is acceptable (yes per "Now" analog). The main fault is the coordination including the fragment c4. Let me reconsider: is k1's conjunct list (c1, c4, c2) — the fragment "Cedar 2" between the statement and the command. The message's "Cedar 2" is what the sign says. Hmm, could one argue that the coordination joining the fragment to the clauses is the only way this formalizer expresses "the content of says"? It's a stretch. A next layer reading k1 with three conjuncts, one a fragment "Cedar 2" — it might interpret Cedar 2 as an utterance content? Not really.

I'm fairly comfortable: L3 wrong conjunct / lost content of "says".

Now write part 4 with rows 75-101 (28 rows: n=180,182,185,186,187,193,197,199,201,202,203,206,209,210,215,218,221,223,224,225,226,227,233,236,238,243,244).

That's 27 rows.
